title: G Protein-Coupled Receptors
terms: Most common cell-surface receptor type; >800 in humans; some act as monomers, some as dimers (transcript). Also called G-protein-linked receptor.
Water-soluble ligands (low octanol:water partition coefficient) can't enter cells; steroids (lipid-soluble, carriers) use cytosolic/nuclear receptors.
Amines (serotonin, ACh, dopamine, histamine), peptides (angiotensin, bradykinin, CCK, oxytocin, vasopressin), chemokines, lipids, glucagon, VIP, GABA/glutamate.
Dogs ~1000 olfactory GPCRs; orphan receptors = GPCRs whose ligands are unknown.
Discovered 1971; cholera and pertussis toxins identified Gs and Gi; Nobel 1994 (Rodbell, Gilman); 2012 crystal structure Nobel.
>800 human GPCR genes; 475 approved drugs (34%, 'a third of all drugs') target 108 GPCRs; 27% of global drug market.
7 transmembrane segments = the SIGNATURE of a GPCR (transcript); N-terminus outside, C-terminus in cytosol.
Domain on the interstitial side that binds the first messenger (e.g., norepinephrine, histamine, acetylcholine).
Intracellular (cytosolic) receptor domain that binds the heterotrimeric G protein.
Long cytoplasmic tail with phosphorylation sites for FEEDBACK regulation; e.g., β-adrenergic receptor kinase changes receptor affinity for norepinephrine.
Three-subunit (α, β, γ) guanine-nucleotide binding protein coupling the GPCR to cytosolic targets: commonly ion channels or enzymes.
Binds GDP/GTP; its GTPase is the TIMER (how long signaling lasts); signals in most pathways (αq, αs, αi).
Dissociates from α when GTP binds; mediates signaling in some pathways (e.g., activates GIRK in Gi pathway).
'Critical slide': G proteins are TIMERS/molecular switches: off (GDP-bound) and on (GTP-bound).
Guanosine diphosphate on α: trimer intact (α with βγ), inactive.
Ligand-bound GPCR acts as an EXCHANGE FACTOR: swaps GTP for GDP; G protein switches on; α and βγ dissociate.
GTPase activity of α = the timer
α hydrolyzes its own GTP → GDP; α re-associates with βγ → off. Signal lasts as long as GTP is bound.
Single-subunit G proteins (~170 known) that are also switches; NOT part of this lecture (transcript).
αq stimulates phospholipase C; ONE pathway with a branch point: IP3/DAG vs NO/cGMP. Historically 'Go (other)'.
G protein whose αs stimulates adenylyl cyclase: cAMP ↑, protein kinase A ↑.
G protein whose αi inhibits adenylyl cyclase: cAMP ↓, protein kinase A ↓.
Other G proteins (GOlf, GGust, transducin, G12, G13)
Additional G proteins for cell and systems physiology; transducin (vision) was the first characterized (transcript).
Intracellular signal made after G protein activation; the 4 prototypical pathways are named for the G protein + second messenger(s).
Cut different bonds of a phospholipid → different products: A1/A2 release fatty acids (arachidonic acid, Basel LC28); C → IP3 + DAG; D.
Stimulated by αq; hydrolyzes PIP2 → IP3 (water-soluble, into cytosol) + DAG (stays in membrane).
Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate: membrane lipid cut by PLC into IP3 + DAG (S15 calls it 'phosphoinositol diphosphate').
Second messenger: opens Ca²⁺ channels on endoplasmic reticulum (slide: receptor-gated channels; transcript says 'ryanodine receptor': see flag).
Stays in the membrane; with Ca²⁺ activates protein kinase C.
Norepinephrine receptor on vascular smooth muscle; Gq/IP3/DAG → contraction = mechanism for NE ↑ vascular resistance (transcript).
Gq α → phospholipase C → IP3 + DAG → ER Ca²⁺ → Ca²⁺-dependent effect (calmodulin); Ca²⁺ + DAG → PKC → phosphorylation effect.
Ligand for α1 (Gq, vascular smooth muscle) and β1 (Gs, pacemaker) receptors.
Intracellular Ca²⁺ store emptied through IP3-gated channels; refilled by SERCA pumps (transcript).
Ca²⁺ sensor giving proteins Ca²⁺ sensitivity; 4 Ca²⁺ sites with COOPERATIVITY → steep curve → essentially all-on/all-off.
Activated by Ca²⁺–CaM; phosphorylates MLC → contraction.
Phosphorylated MLC raises myosin head affinity for actin; cross-bridge cycling needs ATP hydrolysis.
Ca²⁺-dependent kinase activated by DAG + Ca²⁺; phosphorylates CPI-17 → phosphorylation-dependent effect.
Phosphorylated by PKC → INHIBITS MLCP → MLC stays phosphorylated → contraction maintained. Full name NOT required (transcript).
Dephosphorylates MLC → relaxation; inhibited via CPI-17 (Gq/IP3/DAG), activated via MYPT-1 (Gq/NO/cGMP).
IP3 → inositol (slide; transcript: inositol bisphosphate); DAG → phosphatidic acid (or monoacylglycerol, transcript) → ↓ PKC.
Termination: SERCA pumps (Ca²⁺-ATPase) refill the ER + export out of cell (exchangers and pumps).
Histamine receptor on vascular ENDOTHELIUM (transcript); Gq → PLC → IP3 → Ca²⁺ → NO → smooth muscle relaxation.
From mast cells (S18); H1 (Gq/NO/cGMP) → ↓ vascular resistance; H2 (Gs) → stomach acid.
Activated by Ca²⁺; makes NO from the amino acid arginine.
Gaseous messenger; goes to ANOTHER CELL (endothelium → smooth muscle); very short diffusion; oxidized to nitrite/nitrate.
Stimulated by NO; makes cGMP from GTP (same GTP pool the G protein uses, transcript).
Second messenger that stimulates PKG; broken down by phosphodiesterases to GMP.
Phosphorylated by PKG → ACTIVATES myosin light chain phosphatase → relaxation (opposite of CPI-17). Full name NOT required.
NO acts on a different cell (S18)
Endothelial cell (H1, NOS) → NO diffuses → vascular smooth muscle (guanylyl cyclase, PKG) → relaxation. S14 just draws one cell.
'Standing around watching': DAG → PKC → CPI-17 in the same cell would oppose relaxation, so NO acts in another cell.
Norepinephrine receptor in cardiac pacemaker cells; Gs/cAMP → ↑ heart rate.
Stimulated by αs, inhibited by αi; makes cAMP from ATP.
Second messenger; binds HCN directly and the regulatory subunit of PKA ('huge effect on heart rate').
cAMP-dependent kinase; phosphorylates Cav3.x → ↑ open probability → faster depolarization.
Hyperpolarization- and cyclic nucleotide-gated NON-SELECTIVE CATION channel → depolarization (phase 4); cAMP speeds it.
HCN current; 'funny' because it was measured at a non-physiological holding potential (transcript); drives phase 4.
Voltage-sensitive T-type (transient) Ca²⁺ channel; phase 0 upstroke; also in brainstem pacemakers (transcript).
Phase 4 slow depolarization (HCN) → phase 0 upstroke (Cav3.x) → phase 3 repolarization.
Pacemaker: SLOPE of phase 4 sets T-to-P duration → heart rate. Pacemaker cells ≠ contracting cells (transcript).
Break down cAMP → AMP and cGMP → GMP; still active in Gi, so cAMP falls when adenylyl cyclase is inhibited.
Kinases ADD and phosphatases REMOVE phosphates, making enzymes more/less active: 'know that' (transcript).
Acetylcholine receptor in SA node pacemaker cells; Gi: ↓cAMP (HCN, PKA) + βγ → GIRK: three mechanisms → ↓ heart rate.
From the VAGUS (parasympathetic); M2 (Gi, heart), M1/M3 (Gq, bronchi, pancreatic β-cell), M3 (Gq/NO, endothelium).
G protein-gated inwardly rectifying K⁺ channel; βγ opens it → K⁺ out → HYPERPOLARIZATION. 'Put a period on' its importance.
'Four pathways, actually three, one with a branch point' (Gq → IP3/DAG vs NO/cGMP); IP3 arm + DAG arm in one cell.
Same ligand on different receptor subtypes/pathways in different tissues (ACh: M2 vs M3; NE: α1 vs β1).
Different ligands acting on their own receptors in one tissue can activate the same second-messenger cascade.
Mix and match ligand × receptor × G protein pathway → myriad responses; more branch points exist (e.g., arrestin, LC25 RAAS).
Gs/cAMP: arteries vasodilation, bronchi bronchodilation, muscle glycogen breakdown.
V2 = Gs, kidney distal nephron water reabsorption; V1 = Gq/IP3/DAG, arterial vasoconstriction.
Gs appendix receptors: H2, glucagon, ACTH-R, TSH-R
H2 stomach acid; glucagon liver glycogen breakdown; ACTH-R cortisol; TSH-R thyroid hormone.
Gi/cAMP: epinephrine on neurons decreases neurotransmitter release.
Gq/IP3/DAG: ACh bronchoconstriction and insulin secretion; angiotensin arterial vasoconstriction.
traps: CPI-17 vs MYPT-1: CPI-17 is phosphorylated by PKC and INHIBITS MLCP → MLC stays phosphorylated → contraction maintained (S12). MYPT-1 is phosphorylated by PKG and STIMULATES myosin phosphatase → relaxation (S16). Slide says: compare them.
Gq ≠ always contraction: α1 + Gq/IP3/DAG → contraction (S9–S12); H1 + Gq/NO/cGMP → relaxation/vasodilation (S14–S18). Same G protein, same PLC, opposite tone.

Same ligand, different receptor: acetylcholine → M2/Gi heart (↓ rate); M1/M3/Gq/IP3/DAG bronchi (constriction); M3/Gq/NO/cGMP vascular endothelium (vasodilation) (S26, S29). Norepinephrine: α1 (Gq) vessels vs β1 (Gs) heart.
α vs βγ: α carries most signaling and owns the GTPase (S4–S5). βγ activates GIRK in the Gi pathway (S26). On S22 the Gs line 'βγ can activate GIRK/Kir3' is struck through; do not assign GIRK to Gs.
GDP = OFF, GTP = ON: activation = GDP leaves, GTP binds (exchange), not phosphorylation of GDP. Off-switch = α's own GTPase hydrolyzes GTP → GDP (S5).
IP3 vs DAG: IP3 → endoplasmic reticulum channel → Ca²⁺ → CaM → MLCK (S11). DAG + Ca²⁺ → PKC → CPI-17 (S12). Breakdown: IP3 → inositol, DAG → phosphatidic acid ('respectively', S13).

-ase precision: guanylyl cyclase makes cGMP from GTP; adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP; phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP/cGMP to AMP/GMP; phosphatase removes phosphate from proteins; MLCK (kinase) contracts vs MLCP (phosphatase) relaxes.
Direct vs kinase-mediated: cAMP binds HCN directly (faster If); cAMP acts on Cav3.1 via PKA phosphorylation (S22). In Gi, Cav3.1 is changed by phosphatases dephosphorylating it (S26).
Gi lowers cAMP two ways in sequence: αi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, then ongoing phosphodiesterase activity actually drops cAMP (S26). Gi does not destroy cAMP itself.
Kinase per pathway (S6): IP3/DAG → PKC; NO/cGMP → PKG; Gs cAMP ↑ → PKA ↑; Gi cAMP ↓ → PKA ↓. Watch arrows ↑/↓ flipped in options.
Timer = α GTPase, not the receptor: the GPCR is the exchange factor (GDP → GTP, ON); the α subunit's GTPase is the timer (GTP → GDP, OFF) (S5, transcript).
IP3 receptor vs ryanodine receptor: Schultz said 'ryanodine receptor'; slide says receptor-gated channels; textbooks: IP3 receptor (OUTSIDE). Safe answer: IP3-gated Ca²⁺ channel on the ER.
Opening K⁺ hyperpolarizes; HCN depolarizes: GIRK (K⁺ out) = hyperpolarization (Gi); HCN = non-selective cation channel → depolarization (Gs). Don't flip them (transcript).

know.title: G-protein-linked second messenger pathways
know.note: Schultz (transcript): 'four pathways, actually three, one with a branch point'; know the generalized pathways.

know.title: G protein switch: off vs on
know.note: GDP/GTP exchange + subunit dissociation is 'critical for pathway initiation' (S30).
rows: Ligand-activated receptor acts as exchange factor (transcript)
α signals in most pathways; βγ in some
GTP hydrolyzed to GDP by α's own GTPase
α GTPase = the TIMER; signal ends (transcript)

know.title: Four prototypical pathways side by side
know.note: Built from the four pathway slide sets. Say each column top to bottom out loud.
rows: Phospholipase C → NO synthase → guanylyl cyclase
Less PKA; HCN lacks cAMP; βγ → GIRK
αq GTPase; IP3 → inositol, DAG → phosphatidic acid; phosphatases on CPI-17; Ca²⁺ removal
αq GTPase; IP3/DAG breakdown; NO oxidized; PDE: cGMP → GMP; phosphatases on MYPT-1; Ca²⁺ removal
αs GTPase; cAMP leaves HCN/PKA; PDE: cAMP → AMP; phosphatases
αi GTPase; βγ leaves GIRK and rebinds α-GDP

know.title: Appendix: signaling by pathway (ligand / tissue / receptor / response)
know.note: Appendix: 'not an exhaustive table' (transcript). Know the concept (modular system) and recognize entries.
rows: Increase heart rate, contraction velocity, contraction force

quiz.stem: A heterotrimeric G protein has guanosine diphosphate (GDP) bound to its α subunit. Which describes its state? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Switched off, with α and βγ associated
bad: Switched on, with α and βγ dissociated
Switched off, with α and βγ dissociated
Switched on, with α and βγ associated
Partly on, with only βγ free to signal
quiz.why: GDP on α = switched off; the trimer is intact. GTP = on, and α and βγ dissociate.

quiz.stem: Which activity switches a heterotrimeric G protein off by converting guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to guanosine diphosphate (GDP)? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: GTPase activity of the α subunit itself
bad: GTPase activity of the βγ subunit itself
Phosphodiesterase activity in the cytosol
Phosphatase activity acting on the α subunit
Kinase activity at the receptor's cytosolic tail
quiz.why: The α subunit possesses GTPase activity and hydrolyzes its own GTP to GDP, then re-associates with βγ.

quiz.stem: Questions 3–4. A hypothetical drug, vasotonin-X, is a full agonist at α1-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle. Which enzyme does the activated αq subunit stimulate? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Phospholipase C
bad: Phospholipase A2
Phospholipase D
Adenylyl cyclase
Guanylyl cyclase
quiz.why: αq stimulates phospholipase C (PLC), which cleaves phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate (PIP2) into IP3 and DAG.

quiz.stem: (Linked to question 3.) The diacylglycerol (DAG) made in response to vasotonin-X, together with Ca²⁺, activates which kinase, and which protein does that kinase phosphorylate? Key: PKC/PKG/PKA = protein kinase C/G/A; CPI-17 = C-kinase potentiated phosphatase inhibitor; MYPT-1 = myosin phosphatase target 1. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Protein kinase C, which phosphorylates CPI-17
bad: Protein kinase G, which phosphorylates MYPT-1
Protein kinase C, which phosphorylates MYPT-1
Protein kinase A, which phosphorylates CPI-17
Protein kinase G, which phosphorylates CPI-17
quiz.why: DAG + Ca²⁺ activate protein kinase C (PKC), which phosphorylates CPI-17 (C-kinase potentiated protein phosphatase inhibitor, 17 kDa). MYPT-1 is the PKG substrate.

quiz.stem: In α1-adrenergic signaling in vascular smooth muscle, what is the effect of phosphorylated CPI-17? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: It inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase, maintaining contraction
bad: It stimulates myosin light chain phosphatase, causing relaxation
It inhibits myosin light chain kinase, causing relaxation of muscle
It stimulates myosin light chain kinase, initiating contraction
It inhibits guanylyl cyclase, maintaining smooth muscle contraction
quiz.why: Phosphorylated CPI-17 inhibits MLCP, so MLC stays phosphorylated; the DAG pathway reduces relaxation.

quiz.stem: In α1-adrenergic signaling, inositol trisphosphate (IP3) produces contraction through which sequence? Key: ER = endoplasmic reticulum; MLCK/MLCP = myosin light chain kinase/phosphatase; MLC = myosin light chain; NO = nitric oxide; PKG/PKA = protein kinase G/A. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: ER Ca²⁺ release → calmodulin → MLCK → phosphorylated MLC
bad: ER Ca²⁺ release → calmodulin → MLCP → dephosphorylated MLC
ER Ca²⁺ release → NO synthase → PKG → phosphorylated MLC
Cav3.1 Ca²⁺ entry → calmodulin → MLCK → phosphorylated MLC
ER Ca²⁺ release → calmodulin → PKA → phosphorylated MLC
quiz.why: IP3 opens receptor-gated channels on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); Ca²⁺–calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates myosin light chain (MLC).

quiz.stem: Per the lecture, phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) by myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) has which direct effect? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Increases affinity of the myosin head for actin
bad: Decreases affinity of the myosin head for actin
Increases affinity of calmodulin for cytosolic Ca²⁺
Decreases affinity of the phosphatase for its MLC
Increases affinity of the actin filament for CPI-17
quiz.why: Phosphorylated MLC raises myosin head affinity for actin; MLCP dephosphorylation lowers it (relaxation).

quiz.stem: During termination of Gq/IP3/DAG signaling, inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG) are broken down to what, respectively? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Inositol and phosphatidic acid
bad: Phosphatidic acid and inositol
Inositol and arachidonic acid
Glycerol and phosphatidic acid
Inositol and diacylglycerol kinase
quiz.why: S13/S17: 'IP3 and DAG are broken down to inositol and phosphatidic acid, respectively.'

quiz.stem: Which events occur during activation of the Gq/NO/cGMP pathway by histamine at the H1 receptor? Key: NO = nitric oxide; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate; PIP2 = phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol; MYPT-1 = myosin phosphatase target 1. (select all that apply)
ok: Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG
Released Ca²⁺ activates nitric oxide synthase
Nitric oxide stimulates guanylyl cyclase to make cGMP
bad: Nitric oxide synthase makes nitric oxide from glutamine
Phosphorylated MYPT-1 inhibits myosin phosphatase activity
quiz.why: PLC → IP3 → Ca²⁺ → NO synthase (from arginine, not glutamine) → NO → guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → PKG → MYPT-1, which STIMULATES myosin phosphatase. PIP2 = phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate.

quiz.stem: Norepinephrine at α1-adrenergic receptors and histamine at H1 receptors both activate Gq and phospholipase C in the vessel wall. Why do they produce opposite effects on vascular tone? Key: NO = nitric oxide; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate; PKG/PKC = protein kinase G/C; DAG = diacylglycerol. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: H1 signaling adds NO/cGMP/PKG, which stimulates myosin phosphatase
bad: α1 signaling adds NO/cGMP/PKG, which stimulates myosin phosphatase
H1 signaling adds DAG and PKC, which inhibits myosin phosphatase
H1 signaling couples to Gi, which inhibits the adenylyl cyclase
α1 signaling couples to Gs, which activates the adenylyl cyclase
quiz.why: Histamine's Ca²⁺ activates nitric oxide (NO) synthase → cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) → protein kinase G (PKG) → MYPT-1 → myosin phosphatase stimulated → vasodilation.

quiz.stem: How does cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) speed the funny current (If) through the hyperpolarization and cyclic nucleotide gated (HCN) channel in β1-adrenergic signaling? Key: PKA = protein kinase A; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate; GIRK = G protein-gated inwardly rectifying K⁺ channel. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: cAMP binds the HCN channel directly, speeding its activation
bad: PKA phosphorylates the HCN channel, speeding its activation
cAMP binds the Cav3.1 channel directly, speeding its activation
cGMP binds the HCN channel directly, speeding its activation
PKA phosphorylates the GIRK channel, slowing its activation
quiz.why: cAMP binds HCN directly; protein kinase A (PKA) is the route to Cav3.1 (ICa,T), not HCN.

quiz.stem: A hypothetical drug, cardiozine, selectively blocks phosphodiesterases in sinoatrial node pacemaker cells. A dog given cardiozine then receives norepinephrine. Compared with norepinephrine alone, which outcome is expected? Key: cAMP/cGMP = cyclic adenosine/guanosine monophosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: cAMP stays elevated longer, prolonging the heart rate increase
bad: cAMP falls faster, shortening the heart rate increase overall
IP3 stays elevated longer, prolonging the heart rate increase
cAMP stays elevated longer, prolonging the heart rate decrease
cGMP stays elevated longer, prolonging the heart rate increase
quiz.why: β1/Gs raises cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP); phosphodiesterases end the signal by breaking cAMP to AMP. Blocking them prolongs the cAMP-driven ↑ heart rate.

quiz.stem: Norepinephrine has been activating β1-adrenergic Gs/cAMP signaling in cardiac pacemaker cells. Which step is NOT part of terminating this signal? Key: cAMP/AMP = cyclic adenosine/adenosine monophosphate; GTP/GDP = guanosine tri/diphosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Inositol and phosphatidic acid form from IP3 and DAG
bad: The αs subunit hydrolyzes its own bound GTP to GDP
Phosphodiesterases break down the cAMP to form AMP
Phosphatases dephosphorylate target proteins such as the Cav3.1 channel
Norepinephrine dissociates from the β1-adrenergic receptor on the cell
quiz.why: S23 (and transcript): ligand dissociation, αs GTPase, phosphodiesterases (cAMP → AMP), phosphatases. IP3/DAG breakdown is Gq termination, not Gs.

quiz.stem: In an M2 muscarinic receptor pacemaker cell, the αi subunit has just inhibited adenylyl cyclase. What lowers the existing cytosolic cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)? Key: AMP/ATP = adenosine mono/triphosphate; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate; GIRK = G protein-gated inwardly rectifying K⁺ channel. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Ongoing phosphodiesterase activity breaks down the cAMP
bad: The αi subunit directly hydrolyzes the cAMP to AMP
Phosphatases dephosphorylate the cAMP back to ATP
Guanylyl cyclase converts the existing cAMP to cGMP
The βγ subunit exports cAMP out through GIRK channels
quiz.why: αi stops new cAMP synthesis; ongoing phosphodiesterase activity lowers the cAMP already present.

quiz.stem: In the Gi/cAMP pathway in cardiac pacemaker cells, which subunit activates the inwardly rectifying K⁺ (GIRK) channel, and with what effect? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: βγ subunit; hyperpolarization that slows heart rate
bad: αi subunit; hyperpolarization that slows heart rate
βγ subunit; depolarization that speeds heart rate
αs subunit; hyperpolarization that slows heart rate
αi subunit; depolarization that slows the heart rate
quiz.why: The βγ subunit binds and activates GIRK → hyperpolarization; with slower HCN and Cav3.1 activity this decreases heart rate.

quiz.stem: Acetylcholine (ACh) acts on sinoatrial node pacemaker cells, bronchial smooth muscle, and vascular endothelium. Which receptor–pathway–response pairing matches the lecture? Key: NO = nitric oxide; cGMP/cAMP = cyclic guanosine/adenosine monophosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Endothelium: M3 receptor, Gq/NO/cGMP, vasodilation
bad: Pacemaker: M2 receptor, Gq/IP3/DAG, decreased heart rate
Bronchi: M2 receptor, Gi/cAMP, bronchial constriction
Endothelium: M2 receptor, Gi/cAMP, vasodilation
Bronchi: M3 receptor, Gq/NO/cGMP, bronchodilation
quiz.why: ACh: M2/Gi in heart (↓ rate); M1, M3/Gq/IP3/DAG in bronchi (constriction); M3/Gq/NO/cGMP in vascular endothelium (vasodilation). One ligand, many receptor subtypes (S30).

quiz.stem: Which pairing of G protein, second messenger, and major target matches the lecture's summary table? Key: IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol; NO = nitric oxide; cGMP/cAMP = cyclic guanosine/adenosine monophosphate. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Gq → NO/cGMP → protein kinase G
bad: Gs → cAMP ↓ → protein kinase A ↓
Gi → cAMP ↑ → protein kinase A ↑
Gq → IP3/DAG → protein kinase G
Gs → NO/cGMP → protein kinase A
quiz.why: S6: Gq → IP3/DAG → PKC; Gq → NO/cGMP → PKG; Gs → cAMP ↑ → PKA ↑; Gi → cAMP ↓ → PKA ↓. (NO = nitric oxide; cGMP/cAMP = cyclic guanosine/adenosine monophosphate.)

quiz.stem: Which statement about G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) is NOT consistent with the lecture? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: They are single-pass proteins with cytosolic ligand sites
bad: They are seven-pass proteins with extracellular ligand sites
They couple to ion channels or enzymes via G proteins
They are the most common type of cell surface receptor
Their C-terminal tail contains several phosphorylation sites
quiz.why: GPCRs are seven-pass transmembrane proteins with an extracellular ligand-binding site and a cytosolic G protein binding site.

quiz.stem: According to the lecture summary, which statements about G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling are correct? Key: GTP = guanosine triphosphate. (select all that apply)
ok: One ligand can bind receptor subtypes linked to different pathways
Different ligands can activate a common cascade in one cell type
Pathways can bifurcate, causing multiple effects within one cell
bad: Each ligand activates one single pathway in every tissue type
GTP hydrolysis by the α subunit initiates each of the pathways
quiz.why: S30 summary points. GTP hydrolysis ENDS signaling; GDP/GTP exchange and subunit dissociation initiate it. Schultz's framing: a MODULAR system (mix and match ligand × receptor × pathway).

quiz.stem: Vasopressin acts on the kidney distal nephron and on arteries. Which receptor and pathway match each tissue in the lecture appendix? Key: cAMP = cyclic adenosine monophosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol; NO = nitric oxide; cGMP = cyclic guanosine monophosphate. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Kidney V2, Gs/cAMP; arteries V1, Gq/IP3/DAG
bad: Kidney V1, Gs/cAMP; arteries V2, Gq/IP3/DAG
Kidney V2, Gi/cAMP; arteries V1, Gq/NO/cGMP
Kidney V2, Gq/IP3/DAG; arteries V1, Gs/cAMP
Kidney V1, Gq/IP3/DAG; arteries V2, Gs/cAMP
quiz.why: Appendix: V2 (Gs/cAMP) → water reabsorption; V1 (Gq/IP3/DAG) → vasoconstriction. Same ligand, different receptor/pathway = modular system (transcript).

quiz.stem: A hypothetical mutation, αs-Slow, cuts the GTPase activity of αs by 90% in sinoatrial node pacemaker cells. Norepinephrine then binds β1-adrenergic receptors. Compared with normal cells, what is expected? Key: GTP/GDP = guanosine triphosphate/diphosphate. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: Signaling lasts longer because α stays GTP-bound
bad: Signaling ends sooner because α stays GDP-bound
Signaling lasts longer because βγ stays GTP-bound
Signaling never starts because GDP cannot leave α
Signaling ends sooner because the timer runs faster
quiz.why: The α-subunit GTPase is the TIMER: signal lasts as long as GTP is bound. Less GTPase → α stays on longer → prolonged ↑ heart rate.

quiz.stem: In the histamine H1 pathway, diacylglycerol (DAG) is made alongside inositol trisphosphate. Per Dr. Schultz, why must nitric oxide (NO) act on a different cell than the one making it? Key: PKC = protein kinase C; CPI-17 = PKC-potentiated phosphatase inhibitor; MYPT-1 = myosin phosphatase target 1. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: DAG, PKC, and CPI-17 in that cell would oppose relaxation
bad: DAG, PKC, and MYPT-1 in that cell would oppose contraction
NO cannot diffuse at all inside the cell that makes it
Guanylyl cyclase needs a GTP pool separate from G proteins
Calmodulin in that cell would inhibit nitric oxide synthase
quiz.why: DAG is 'standing around watching.' If DAG → PKC → CPI-17 inhibited myosin light chain phosphatase in the same cell, it would block relaxation; so NO goes from endothelium to smooth muscle. Guanylyl cyclase uses the SAME GTP pool.

quiz.stem: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve binds M2 muscarinic receptors on sinoatrial node pacemaker cells. Which mechanisms slow the heart rate? Key: GIRK = G protein-gated inwardly rectifying K⁺ channel; cAMP = cyclic adenosine monophosphate; HCN = hyperpolarization- and cyclic nucleotide-gated channel; PKA = protein kinase A. (select all that apply)
ok: βγ opens GIRK channels, hyperpolarizing the cell
Lower cAMP decreases HCN channel activity
Lower PKA activity reduces Cav3.x phosphorylation
bad: βγ closes GIRK channels, depolarizing the cell
αi activates phosphodiesterase, destroying cAMP
quiz.why: THREE mechanisms: βγ → GIRK (K⁺ out → hyperpolarization); ↓cAMP → ↓HCN; ↓cAMP → ↓PKA → less Cav3.x phosphorylation (phosphatases still active). αi INHIBITS adenylyl cyclase; phosphodiesterase is simply still active.

quiz.stem: Dr. Schultz said to know the generalized Gq pathway. Which sequence matches it? Key: PLC = phospholipase C; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate; DAG = diacylglycerol; ER = endoplasmic reticulum; PKC/PKA = protein kinase C/A. (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: αq → PLC → IP3 + DAG → ER Ca²⁺ release → PKC
bad: αq → adenylyl cyclase → IP3 + DAG → ER Ca²⁺ release → PKC
αq → PLC → cAMP + DAG → ER Ca²⁺ release → PKC

quiz.stem: Calmodulin has four Ca²⁺ binding sites that bind with cooperativity. What does this cooperativity produce for Ca²⁺-sensitive targets such as myosin light chain kinase? (select one correct response)
quiz.ok: A steep activation curve: essentially all-on or all-off
bad: A shallow activation curve: finely graded with Ca²⁺ level

A shallow activation curve: one site saturates first
A steep activation curve: requires a single Ca²⁺ only
quiz.why: Cooperativity between multiple binding sites steepens the concentration-dependence curve, so calmodulin is essentially all-on or all-off.
